claims.text: Increasing atomic size mismatch in single-phase FCC CoCrFeMnNi-based alloys increases local lattice distortion.
Adding 1–5 at.% Ti can increase atomic size misfit in CoCrFeMnNi-based alloys.
Adding 1–5 at.% Al can reduce atomic size misfit in CoCrFeMnNi-based alloys.
Local lattice distortions raise the energy barriers for dislocation motion.
Higher barriers to dislocation motion increase hardness and yield strength relative to a low-mismatch baseline.
Arc melting followed by homogenization at approximately 1200°C for 24 hours and water quenching establishes a consistent single-phase FCC baseline microstructure.
Atomic size mismatch can be varied by adding Ti or Al while valence electron concentration and mixing entropy remain nearly constant.
Variations in lattice parameters measured by XRD quantify local lattice distortions.
Increased dislocation density and strain fields observed by TEM are indicators of increased local lattice distortion.
Lattice distortions caused by atomic size mismatch act as barriers to dislocation glide.
Inhibition of dislocation glide raises both yield strength and hardness.
Alloys with higher atomic size misfit will have significantly greater hardness and yield strength than the baseline alloy.
Alloys with higher atomic size misfit will exhibit stronger local strain fields and more dislocation pinning in TEM than the baseline.
If secondary phases and ordering remain unchanged, mechanical enhancement can be attributed to increased lattice distortion.
The proposed relationship is expected to hold for single-phase FCC high-entropy alloys containing 1–5 at.% additions and tested at room temperature.
More extensive alloying or different heat treatments may produce secondary phases or chemical ordering that invalidate the proposed attribution.
Subtle secondary phases or chemical ordering may occur even at small alloying additions and affect mechanical properties.

contradictions.description: The intervention is framed as a controlled increase in atomic size mismatch, but Al is described as reducing misfit. A misfit-reducing addition does not directly test the stated higher-misfit prediction unless it is explicitly designated as a reverse-trend control.

The boundary excludes alloys in which secondary phases or ordering develop, whereas the falsification rule treats observation of those features as falsification. Such an observation would ordinarily place the experiment outside the stated domain rather than falsify the within-domain mechanism.
